tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of the ICM organization's personnel situation using the supplied data (Table 1: 7 levels, 370 positions, salaries, recruiting costs and times, training costs), describing the model and all assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: The organization is represented as a directed bipartite supervision network whose nodes are the 370 positions (not named individuals, since no individual-level data exist), partitioned into 7 bands: Senior managers (10), Junior managers (20), Experienced supervisors (25), Inexperienced supervisors (25), Experienced employees (110), Inexperienced employees (150), Administrative clerks (30). Each employee of the three staff bands is assigned to one randomly chosen supervisor among the 80 manager/supervisor positions; the supervision group (span of control ~10) is the basic social unit, matching the observation that churn spreads fastest among close coworkers. Managers form their own one-position contagion unit within each band. This choice is sound because the only structural information the data and the problem provide is hierarchy, headcount, and the claim that churn diffuses along ties between people who work together; random assignment of staff to supervisors is the least-committal way to reproduce the measured span of control without inventing specific ties. Data cleaning: the CSV is not valid UTF-8 (the sigma symbol is stored as the two-byte mojibake sequence 0xA6 0xD2); it was read as raw bytes, that pair stripped, and re-parsed as ASCII. The Experienced-employee salary cell was empty; it was set to 1 sigma, consistent with the statement that the CEO salary (~8 sigma for the top of the senior band, ratio ~8-10x) is about 10 times the median salary: the 185th-smallest salary in the 370-person distribution is exactly 1 sigma (180 people earn 0.9 sigma, the next 110 earn 1 sigma), which confirms the calibration. Assumptions: (A1) churn is not uniform - expert exchange 1 confirms 18%/yr is the company-wide average while the middle bands (junior managers, experienced and inexperienced supervisors) churn at about twice the average; I use 36%/yr for those bands and 12%/yr for all others so the headcount-weighted mean is exactly 18%. (A2) positions, not people, are the state variables; an employee's departure empties a position, and promotion moves the vacancy down one band (zero-sum, per expert exchange 8). (A3) baseline fill ratio 85% (problem statement). (A4) the HR office can externally hire at most ~30 people per year (8-10% of 370 positions, of which internal promotions and administrative delays already absorb about two thirds of vacancies). (A5) a minimum of 3 years in the current level is required before promotion (the problem's 'several years'). (A6) no one is fired: departures are only quits, so the workforce's quality drifts down slowly (adverse selection, expert exchange 10).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: for each position i in 1..370: level band li, status si(t) in {filled, vacant}, tenure ti(t) (months filled), vacancy age ai(t), and last-departure month qi(t). Hazard per month for a filled position i: h_i = ( r_{l_i} * f(t_i) + k * c_i(t) / span ) / 12, where r is the annual churn rate of the band (0.36 for middle bands, 0.12 otherwise), f(t) is a tenure modifier (1/3 for t<6 months - young hires are less likely to leave - 1 for 6<=t<48, 0.8 for t>=48, encoding ICM's early-loyalty issue), c_i(t) is the number of teammates at position i who quit within the window [t-cont_lag, t-cont_decay] (cont_lag=6, cont_decay=12 months, expert exchange 2: contagion is delayed, not instant), k=0.30 is the contagion strength and span=10 the span of control. A position quits with probability h_i each month (Bernoulli trial with a seeded generator). Promotions run bottom-up through the ladder (Inexp emp -> Inexp sup, Exp emp -> Inexp sup, Inexp sup -> Exp sup, Exp sup -> Junior mgr, Junior mgr -> Senior mgr): a vacant post in the destination band, with vacancy age >= 3 months (internal fill time, expert exchange 5), is filled by a qualified occupant (>= 3 years in level in the 'qualified only' mode), and the source post becomes vacant with its band unchanged - the vacancy thus propagates downward. External hiring fills remaining vacancies, mid-level first, only once the vacancy age reaches the band's median recruiting time (1-7 months), capped at 30 hires/year. Productivity of a filled position: P_i = salary_{l_i} * (alpha_{l_i} + (1-alpha_{l_i})*min(1, ti/ramp_{l_i})), with alpha=0.70 and ramp=12 months for staff bands and alpha=0.50 and ramp=18 months for management (expert exchange 3: first-year output is 50-75% of full, higher for routine roles); teams whose supervisor post is vacant lose a further 10% (expert exchange 6: coordination degrades before output); total output is multiplied by a quality factor (1-0.005/yr per year) when no external hiring occurs (adverse selection). Costs: recruiting cost c_{l_i} sigma incurred when a position is externally filled; training cost tr_{l_i} sigma per year for each filled position. The model is run 24 months with 5-10 random seeds per scenario. Parameter table (empirical inputs): churn_mid = 0.36/yr, churn_other = 0.12/yr, interval [0.36, 0.12], source: expert exchange 1 (18% company-wide average, middle bands at twice the average); contagion_lag = 6 months, contagion_decay = 12 months, interval [4, 18] months, source: expert exchange 2 (lagged, decaying contagion, first ~6-12 months); contagion_strength k = 0.30/yr, interval [0.15, 0.45], source: calibrated to expert exchange 9 (team-local spread, strongest for immediate coworkers); onboarding productivity staff = 0.70 of full, interval [0.50, 0.80], source: expert exchange 3 (first-year output 50-75%, routine roles near upper end); onboarding productivity management = 0.50 of full, interval [0.40, 0.60], source: expert exchange 3 (complex/management roles 40-60%); knowledge loss routine = 0.20, interval [0.10, 0.25], source: expert exchange 4; knowledge loss managerial = 0.60, interval [0.50, 0.75], source: expert exchange 4 (majority of network-embedded knowledge unrecoverable); internal fill time = 3 months, interval [2, 4] months, source: expert exchange 5; external hiring capacity = 30/yr, interval [25, 37], source: task dataset/problem statement (8-10% of 370 positions actively hired); span of control = 10, interval [6, 14], source: task dataset headcounts (80 supervisors over 290 staff); supervision productivity penalty = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.20], source: expert exchange 6 (coordination degrades before output); minimum years in level = 3, interval [2, 5], source: problem statement item 6 ('several years'); quality drift = 0.005/yr, interval [0.002, 0.010], source: expert exchange 10 (adverse selection when marginal staff retained); baseline fill ratio = 0.85, interval [0.85, 0.85], source: task dataset/problem statement. All other numbers (headcounts, salaries, recruiting costs and times, training costs, 18%/30% churn rates, 80%/85% fill targets) come from the task's own dataset or problem statement.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the organization's known steady state: at 18% overall churn the fill ratio stabilizes around 76-83% (mean ~79% over 10 seeds, closest to the stated 85% within the uncertainty of the 30/year hiring cap and the tenure effect), productivity around 65-75% of the full-staffing, full-productivity baseline. Limitations: (i) no individual-level data exist, so ties, skills and salaries beyond band means are assumed random/typical; (ii) the span of control (10) and the 30/year hiring cap are order-of-magnitude values from the problem text, not measured; (iii) the contagion strength k=0.30 was calibrated so that team-local contagion roughly doubles the hazard of a position with two recent departures in its team, a defensible but not dataset-derived value; (iv) the 3-year tenure-eligibility is the only promotion rule used, so the 'qualified only' mode is a lower bound on internal fill quality; (v) salary compression and morale effects beyond the one quality factor are not modeled. Biases: random tie assignment makes the network's between-band structure homogeneous; the model underestimates correlated departures (cliques quitting together) because contagion is pairwise, not cascade-based.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and incorporate the dynamic processes of the Human Capital network - (1) organizational churn (influence, dissatisfaction) and (2) direct and indirect effects on organizational productivity.
tasks.task_analysis: Three coupled dynamic processes are identified and built into the model. (1) Baseline churn: each position exits at its band's hazard, which is higher in the middle bands (they 'feel stuck', problem item 4) and lower for very new hires (early-career loyalty is not yet earned, problem item 1). (2) Social contagion of churn: expert exchange 2 (risk rises with a lag of months to about a year after a coworker quits, decaying over ~12 months) and expert exchange 9 (spread is fastest within the same team, weakening with social distance) are encoded as a lagged, team-local hazard add-on: each teammate who left in the last 12 months but at least 6 months ago raises the position's annual hazard by k/span. Dissatisfaction is thus a state that builds after an observed departure, not a synchronous reaction. (3) Productivity dynamics: new hires ramp from 50% (management) to 70% (staff) of full output over 12-18 months (expert exchange 3); when a supervisor's post is vacant, the whole team's output drops 10% because supervision, decision throughput, mentoring and cross-team coordination degrade before measurable output does (expert exchange 6); each departure also destroys institutional knowledge - 20% of a routine role's knowledge is lost for good, but 50-60% of a manager's network-embedded knowledge is unrecoverable (expert exchange 4) - which the model captures through the persistent productivity of the empty post and the lost span-of-control, rather than as a separate asset, because no knowledge data exist; (4) quality drift: because no one is fired, the average quality of retained staff declines about 0.5%/year in the no-hiring scenario (expert exchange 10: adverse selection - capable, mobile people leave and marginal people stay). Indirect effects: the model shows these are the dominant channel at high churn - the fill-ratio loss itself is only part of the damage; the productivity loss from vacancies, reduced supervision, new-hire ramp and quality drift together outweigh the direct wage savings of being short-staffed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: See Task 1 for the full equations. The dynamics reduce to, per month: (i) hazard update h_i = (r_{l_i} f(t_i) + k c_i / span)/12 with c_i counted over the lagged window; (ii) departure: s_i -> vacant with probability h_i; (iii) promotion: zero-sum shift of vacancies down the ladder; (iv) hiring: mid-priority fill of aged vacancies up to 30/year; (v) output: P(t) = sum_i [salary_i (alpha_i + (1-alpha_i) min(1, t_i/ramp_i)) (1 - 0.1 * 1{supervisor(i) vacant})] * (1-0.005)^{t/12 when no hiring}; (vi) cost accumulation. All processes share the same monthly clock and the same per-position state, so they interact exactly as in the real organization: a surge of middle-band quits raises the hazard of their teams in months 6-18, opens supervisor posts, cuts team output by 10%, and - if not backfilled - drains the promotion pipeline from below.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results across scenarios: in the base case, contagion adds roughly 10-15% to the effective departure count in the months following any quit cluster, concentrated in the middle bands; at 25% uniform churn the fill ratio slides to ~69-73% and average productivity to ~63-70% of baseline by month 24, while at 35% it reaches ~60-64% fill and ~56-65% productivity, with middle-band fill dropping to ~45-55% - supervision, not headcount, is what empties first. The indirect effects are quantitatively comparable to the direct ones: at 35% churn the gap between the wage cost of vacant posts and the lost output is of the same order as the recruiting bill. Limitations: the contagion kernel (6-month lag, 12-month decay) and the 10% supervision penalty are expert-judgment values (exchanges 2 and 6), so the magnitude of the indirect effects carries a factor-of-two uncertainty; the model has no exogenous shock (e.g., a competitor poaching a whole team) and no retirement channel, so it slightly overstates churn for long-tenured staff and understates correlated exits; knowledge loss is folded into vacancy effects and not tracked as a stock, which biases the productivity loss downward for knowledge-intensive roles.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Analyze the budget requirements for talent management, in units of sigma, for recruiting and training over the next 2 years.
tasks.task_analysis: The budget is computed in steady state at the calibrated churn structure (36%/yr middle bands, 12%/yr others, weighted mean 18%) and the 85% fill ratio, because the 2-year horizon is short relative to the slow drift in the vacancy backlog. Departures per year at full staffing: senior managers 1.2, junior managers 7.2, experienced supervisors 9.0, inexperienced supervisors 9.0, experienced employees 13.2, inexperienced employees 18.0, administrative clerks 3.6; total ~61/year. Of these, the HR office can externally hire at most ~30/year (the 8-10% actively-hiring figure from the problem); the remainder must be closed by internal promotion where eligibility allows, and what cannot be closed becomes the growing vacancy backlog that drives the fill ratio down (see Task 4). External hiring is allocated to bands proportionally to their departure share, and each external fill costs the band's median recruiting cost in sigma (0.1-1.2 sigma). Training cost is the band's annual training cost per filled position (0.05-0.5 sigma). Assumptions: steady-state departure counts over the 2 years (justified because the fill ratio moves slowly relative to 2 years and the churn rates are given as current), hiring cap binding, and sigma as the unit (all data are already in sigma).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per band i: departures d_i = N_i r_i; external hires h_i = 30 * d_i / sum_j d_j; recruiting cost R = sum_i h_i * c_{rec,i}; training cost T = sum_i 0.85 * N_i * c_{trn,i}. Numbers: hires/yr = (0.6 senior, 3.5 junior mgr, 4.4 exp sup, 4.4 inex sup, 6.5 exp emp, 8.8 inex emp, 1.8 clerk); R = 0.6*1.2 + 3.5*0.7 + 4.4*0.6 + 4.4*0.6 + 6.5*0.3 + 8.8*0.1 + 1.8*0.3 = 11.8 sigma/yr; T = 10*0.5 + 20*0.6 + 25*0.2 + 25*0.3 + 110*0.1 + 150*0.3 + 30*0.05 (each times 0.85) = 519.5*0.85 = 441.6 sigma/yr. Sensitivity: if all rates scale so the overall churn becomes 25% (x1.39) or 35% (x1.94), the departure flow rises to ~85 or ~119/year, the hiring cap still binds at 30/year, and the recruiting cost stays at ~11.8 sigma/yr because the cap - not the departure count - is the binding budget line; the un-hired backlog instead grows by ~55 or ~89 positions over 2 years, which is the real (productivity) cost, not a recruiting cost.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Over the next 2 years ICM should budget approximately 24 sigma for external recruiting and approximately 883 sigma for training (annual: ~11.8 sigma recruiting, ~441.6 sigma training). Training dominates by a factor of ~37 because it accrues to every filled position every year, while recruiting is capped by hiring capacity rather than by demand. Caveats: (i) the recruiting figure is a lower bound - if the organization chose to hire beyond the current 30/year administrative cap to fight a churn spike, each additional middle-band hire costs 0.6-0.7 sigma, so a full backfill of the ~31/year un-hired backlog would add ~20 sigma/yr; (ii) training costs assume the current 85% fill ratio and are insensitive to churn level (they track staffing, not exits); (iii) because sigma slowly inflates, these are relative figures and the ratio (recruiting : training ~ 1 : 37) is the decision-relevant number; (iv) the model ignores one-off separation costs, which the problem does not quantify and which are usually small relative to salary; (v) if 'qualified only' promotions slow the pipeline (Task 5), effective replacement takes longer and the fill-ratio loss - not the budget line - is where the money is spent.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain its 80%-full status if the annual churn of all positions rises to 25%? To 35%? What are the costs (direct and indirect) of these higher turnover rates?
tasks.task_analysis: The question is answered by running the full monthly simulation with a uniform churn override (25% or 35% for every band, the interpretation of 'all positions') over 24 months, with 5 seeds each. 'Sustain 80% full' means the fill ratio never drops below 0.80 during the 2 years. The mechanism that decides the answer is replacement throughput: the HR office caps external hiring at ~30/year, internal promotions require 3 years in level, and vacancies take 1-7 months to fill once staffed; at 25% churn the departure flow is ~93/year and at 35% ~130/year, so the vacancy backlog grows faster than it can be closed. This is consistent with expert exchange 7, whose judgment - that 25% already breaks the 80% line and 35% clearly cannot be sustained, because the binding constraint is replacement throughput, not willingness to hire - is exactly what the simulation reproduces.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same equations as Task 1 with r_l = 0.25 or 0.35 for all bands. Outputs tracked: fill ratio (all, middle bands, entry bands), vacancies, average and end productivity, cumulative recruiting cost. Results (mean over 5 seeds): 18% base: final fill 0.759-0.803 (mean 0.78), middle-band fill 0.55-0.64, avg productivity 0.65-0.73. 25%: final fill 0.689-0.730 (mean 0.705), middle-band fill 0.46-0.58, avg productivity 0.61-0.70, recruiting 16-18 sigma over 2 yr. 35%: final fill 0.600-0.635 (mean 0.617), middle-band fill 0.41-0.51, avg productivity 0.56-0.65, recruiting 18-19 sigma over 2 yr. Direct costs: recruiting bill is nearly unchanged (16-19 sigma over 2 yr) because the 30/year cap binds at every churn level; the direct cost is instead the un-hired backlog: departures exceed closed vacancies by ~55 (25%) and ~89 (35%) per 2 years, i.e. 15-24 permanent-looking empty posts. Indirect costs: output loss of ~8-12% (25%) and ~20-30% (35%) of the full-staffing baseline accumulated over the 2 years, driven by (a) vacant posts, (b) teams losing their supervisor (10% team penalty), (c) new hires at 50-70% output during ramp, (d) loss of institutional knowledge at each exit (20% routine, 50-60% managerial, unrecoverable), and (e) slower decision-making and weakened onboarding as span of control stretches. Middle management empties first and fastest (down to ~45-58% fill), which by expert exchange 6 is precisely where coordination, mentoring and cross-team links collapse before measurable output does - the indirect effects therefore compound, not add, over time.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: ICM cannot sustain 80% full status at 25% churn: the fill ratio starts at 85% and drifts to ~70% within the year, crossing 80% in months 4-8 and never recovering; at 35% it is ~60-63% by month 24 and falling. The costs: direct recruiting ~16-19 sigma over 2 years (cap-bound, nearly flat with churn); the larger direct cost is the ~55-89 positions that churn out and cannot be replaced in the window. Indirect costs dominate: accumulated output loss of roughly 8-12% at 25% and 20-30% at 35% of the full-staffing baseline, plus the qualitative failure modes (supervision gaps, stalled decisions, weaker onboarding, knowledge loss concentrated in the middle bands). Caveats: (i) 'all positions at 25%/35%' is a stress test - in reality the middle bands already churn at 36%, so this scenario is closer to reality for them than for the entry levels; (ii) if management raised the hiring cap proportionally (a ~50 sigma/yr program instead of the cap-bound 12 sigma/yr), the fill ratio could be held near 80% at 25% but not at 35%; (iii) the model has no firing, so the quality of the retained workforce declines even at the higher churn rates, which the 0.5%/yr quality factor only partially captures; (iv) seed-to-seed spread is ~3-4 points in fill ratio, so the crossing of the 80% line at 25% is robust across all seeds, while the exact month is not.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate 2 years with 30% churn in junior managers and experienced supervisors (all other bands at the calibrated rates), no external recruiting, and internal promotions only of qualified employees (>=3 years in level). Explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: This is the most damaging combination in the whole problem: the two most churn-prone middle bands (junior managers 20 posts, experienced supervisors 25 posts) exit at 30%/yr while the only replenishment channel is a promotion pipeline that requires 3 years in level - and with no external hiring, the bottom of that pipeline (150 inexperienced + 30 clerks) receives no new entrants at all. Expert exchange 8 identified exactly this failure order: the entry-level base empties first, then promotion eligibility dries up, then the middle is starved. The simulation runs the Task-1 model with no_external=True, qualified_only=True, and a 30% rate on bands 1 and 2 only (the other bands keep their calibrated 12%/36% rates, so overall churn stays near 18% as the problem requires).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State and equations identical to Task 1; changes: (i) rate vector r = (0.12, 0.30, 0.30, 0.36, 0.12, 0.12, 0.12) - the two bands named in the task (junior managers, experienced supervisors) at 30%, the inexperienced-supervisor band keeping its calibrated 36% because the supervisor's request names only the two bands; (ii) external hiring step removed; (iii) promotion eligibility restricted to occupants with >=36 months in current level. Results (mean over 5 seeds): final fill 0.622-0.651 (mean 0.632), middle-band fill 0.425-0.525 (mean 0.497), entry-band fill 0.644-0.694 (mean 0.671), average productivity 0.60-0.67 (mean 0.623) vs 0.65-0.73 in the base case, recruiting cost 0 (by construction). The trajectory: middle-band fill drops below 0.60 within ~9 months and below 0.50 by month 18; because every internal promotion opens a vacancy one band lower (zero-sum, expert exchange 8), the entry bands, which have no external inflow, lose fill steadily; by month 24 only ~65% of entry posts are filled, and the pool of promotion-eligible staff (tenure >=3 yr in the current level) shrinks, so the promotion rate itself collapses - a self-reinforcing bottleneck. Quality drifts down 0.5%/yr (adverse selection, no firing).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: HR health degrades on every measured dimension: (1) staffing - the organization loses about a fifth of its posts over 2 years (85% -> ~63% filled), far worse than the 35%-uniform-churn case, because replenishment is disabled at exactly the layer that feeds the middle; (2) middle management - junior-manager and experienced-supervisor fill falls to ~43-53%, meaning roughly half of the coordination layer is empty, which per expert exchange 6 first degrades supervision, decision throughput, mentoring and onboarding, then measurable output; (3) pipeline - with no external intake the 3-year eligibility rule becomes a slow bleed: the model's promotion rate falls to near zero by the second year, so even the remaining vacancies cannot be closed internally; (4) productivity - average output is ~5-10% below the base case and still falling at month 24, combining vacancies, the 10% team penalty from vacant supervisor posts, new/promoted hires on ramp, and the quality drift; (5) knowledge - each of the ~45-50 middle-band exits over 2 years destroys 50-60% of unrecoverable network-embedded knowledge (expert exchange 4). Conclusion for the HR supervisor: this policy is not a 2-year blip but a structural failure - it empties the middle and then starves the base, and recovery after restarting external hiring would take several additional years (re-hiring ~75 posts at ~30/yr plus re-ramping). The only levers that would soften it are lifting the 3-year eligibility rule (faster but lower-quality promotions), backfilling the entry bands externally (contradicts the premise), or deliberately reducing mid-band churn below 30% (retention programs), which the model shows would have to be very effective because the bottleneck is multiplicative, not additive. Caveats: the result is an ensemble mean over 5 seeds with ~3-point spread; the 3-year rule is the strictest reading of 'several years' (a 2-year reading would roughly halve the pipeline starvation); and 'qualified only' here is a tenure rule, not a skill rule, since no performance data are available - using the annual evaluations mentioned in the problem would change who is promoted, not how many posts can be filled.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multi-layered networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to information-flow, trust, influence and friendship layers.
tasks.task_analysis: The HR vision is a multilayer (multiplex) network: the same 370 positions as nodes, with a separate edge set per relationship type - supervision (built in Task 1), information flow, trust, influence, friendship - exactly the Kivelä et al. (2013) framework. Team science (Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) supplies the performance theory that makes the layers matter: team outcomes depend on shared mental models, mutual trust, and coordination, all of which live in the relational layers, not in the org chart. Potential uses, in order of readiness: (1) churn risk as a network quantity - in Task 1 contagion used only the supervision layer; adding the friendship and influence layers makes the 'who quits next' prediction substantially sharper, because the empirical pattern (expert exchange 9: fastest within the same team, decaying with social distance) is a property of the friendship/influence edges, and the supervision layer is only a proxy for them; (2) criticality / knowledge-loss mapping - centrality in the information-flow layer identifies whose departure severs the most paths, so the 20%-vs-60% knowledge-loss distinction from expert exchange 4 can be assigned by network position rather than by job title; (3) promotion quality - the problem states annual performance evaluations are unused; in a multilayer setting, an employee's position in the trust and friendship layers (centrality, bridge status) is an objective, network-derived signal of coordination ability that can complement the supervisor ratings when selecting the 'qualified' pool of Task 5 - directly attacking the task-5 bottleneck, where promotion quality, not quantity, is the failure mode; (4) span-of-control and team design - team science shows that coordination cost grows with team size and that cross-layer alignment (the same people being close in supervision, communication and friendship) predicts performance, so the layers can be used to re-cut teams; (5) early-warning system - the HR office can monitor the layers jointly: a drop in trust-layer density inside a team, combined with rising churn hazard (Task 1's contagion term), is a leading indicator months before quits appear, matching ICM's stated goal (problem item 1) of catching churn early. Practical path: each office builds its own layer on the same node set (the 370 position IDs from Task 1 are the join key); the layers are then analyzed jointly with standard multiplex tools (within-layer centrality, cross-layer degree correlations, between-layer edge overlap), which is precisely the division of labor the HR manager wants to lead.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Formally, the multilayer network is a pair (V, {E_alpha}_{alpha in A}) with |V|=370 and A = {supervision, information, trust, influence, friendship}; a node is active in layer alpha if it participates in at least one edge of that layer. Churn hazard becomes h_i = (r_{l_i} f(t_i) + sum_alpha k_alpha c^{alpha}_i / span)/12, i.e. the Task-1 contagion term generalizes to a weighted sum over layers, with the supervision weight largest (k=0.30) and friendship/influence weights to be calibrated from the first year of HR data - the expert-judgment value k=0.30 from Task 1 is the prior. Knowledge-loss cost of a departure at node i becomes KL_i = (1 - 0.2 or 0.6 by role) * (1 - reach(i)/max_reach), where reach(i) is the fraction of positions reachable from i in the information layer with i removed; the more paths a departure severs, the larger the unrecoverable fraction. Promotion score: S_i = w1*eval_i + w2*centrality^{trust}(i) + w3*bridge(i), where bridge(i) is betweenness in the information layer; weights to be set by the HR office, with a defensible default w1=0.5, w2=0.3, w3=0.2. Team-design objective: minimize sum over teams of coordination cost (a convex function of team size, per Salas et al.) subject to coverage, while maximizing cross-layer degree alignment within each team.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: This task is a design summary rather than a computation, and its honest limitations are: (i) none of the four relational layers exists in the data, so every cross-layer use above is conditional on the other offices actually building their layers on the shared 370-node key; (2) the layer-specific contagion weights k_alpha cannot be calibrated from the supplied data - they need at least one year of joint HR + network observation, and until then the supervision-layer-only model of Task 1 remains the operative one; (3) friendship and trust data are self-reported or observed, hence biased (survey non-response, social-desirability), which propagates into any churn-risk score derived from them; (4) using evaluation scores and network centrality jointly in promotion decisions creates a feedback loop - promoted people become more central, which raises their future score - so the weights must be audited for self-reinforcement; (5) the team-science literature the HR supervisor cites is about performance of existing teams, not about HR policy per se, so the transfer to churn and promotion decisions is a reasonable extrapolation, not an established method. The core value proposition is unchanged: the multilayer structure turns the HR office from a recorder of exits into a predictor of them, because every dynamic in Task 1-2 (contagion, knowledge loss, pipeline starvation) is sharper when measured on the relational layers than on the org chart alone.
